title: Roast Sirloin of Beef
subtitle: Salt-rubbed, rested, and served pink
excerpt: A British Sunday roast centrepiece: sirloin joint seasoned generously, seared to colour, then roasted at a controlled temperature and rested until the juices settle. Serve with Yorkshire puddings and roast potatoes.

recipe.sourceNotes: Roast beef is the dish most associated with English cooking, to the point where the French nickname for the English is les rosbifs. The sirloin is a cut from the back of the animal, behind the ribs, with a distinctive fat cap that bastes the meat as it roasts. The word sirloin derives from the Old French surlonge (above the loin), though a popular story attributes it to a knighting by a British king who was so impressed by the cut that he conferred a knighthood upon it. The tradition of the Sunday roast developed in England as a consequence of the working week: butchers sold joints on Saturday, and the joint went into the oven before church on Sunday, ready for the midday meal on return. A properly rested sirloin, served pink, with horseradish cream and a Yorkshire pudding, remains one of the defining dishes of the British table.

recipeTools.notes: A heavy roasting tin large enough to hold the joint without crowding.

content.text: Rest the meat for at least 20 minutes after it comes out of the oven: this is not optional. The fibres contract during cooking and relax on resting, drawing the juices back through the meat. A joint carved too soon will bleed onto the board. Use an instant-read thermometer for accuracy: 52 to 55 C internal for rare, 57 to 60 C for medium-rare, 65 C for medium.

items.preparation: boned and rolled, or bone-in; at room temperature for 1 hour before cooking

content.text: Heat the oven to 220 C (200 C fan). Pat the joint dry, rub all over with oil, then season generously with salt and pepper. Place fat-side up in the roasting tin.

Roast at 220 C for 20 minutes to colour the outside. Reduce the temperature to 160 C (140 C fan) and continue roasting: allow 12 to 14 minutes per 500 g for rare, 16 to 18 minutes per 500 g for medium-rare. A 1.5 kg boned joint needs roughly 40 to 50 minutes at the lower temperature after the initial blast.

Remove the joint when the internal temperature reads 52 to 55 C for rare or 57 to 60 C for medium-rare. Transfer to a warm board, cover loosely with foil, and rest for at least 20 minutes before carving. The temperature will rise by 3 to 5 C during resting. Use the roasting juices to make a red-wine gravy.
